title: Basic Intergluteal Numismatics

jokes.text: Please stay for complimentary saltines and full-price sodas.
jokes.setup: An announcement promising a complimentary refreshment, implying generosity
jokes.punchline: The 'complimentary' item is saltines — the cheapest possible food — while sodas remain full-price, inverting any sense of hospitality
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton economy-of-means joke. The specificity of 'saltines' does the heavy lifting — it's not just 'cheap food,' it's the most pointlessly minimal hospitality gesture possible. Tight, in-character, and sets the Greendale-is-terrible tone efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Those are some really good crackers.

jokes.text: But first, the dulcet tones of The Bennett Boys.
jokes.setup: An MC-style introduction implying a polished, pleasant musical act
jokes.punchline: The band plays 'Creep' by Radiohead — an ominous, melancholy song utterly inappropriate for a school pep event, made funnier by the pompous 'dulcet tones' framing
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the juxtaposition: the formal, grandiose introduction ('dulcet tones') against the song that follows, which is Radiohead's 'Creep' — a song about being a creep and a weirdo. Foreshadows the Ass Crack Bandit's return with tonal perfection. The rewatch bonus is high because on rewatch the song choice reads as an intentional thematic statement about the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Et tu, Brute? You were supposed to be there for me!

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: We've been through so much together, and you just... break on me now?

jokes.text: Hey, bro, free crackers. Wanna spend your life opening lockers? / You don't have to raise your voice! I'm going as fast as I can!
jokes.setup: Someone excitedly tells their friend about free crackers at a mundane school event
jokes.punchline: Garrett, apparently a locker-room attendant, is being yelled at for going too slow and snaps defensively — the mundane indignity of Garrett's life at Greendale is the joke
jokes.explanation: Garrett is a reliable background-character punching bag and this is a solid use of him. The specificity of 'opening lockers' as his life's purpose is funny. Not exceptional writing but competently deployed.

dialogue.line: Overly dramatic cliché applied to trivial problems

jokes.text: Oh, great, now I have these folders to deal with! / Et tu, pencil? / When it rains, it pours.
jokes.setup: Garrett is already overwhelmed and complaining
jokes.punchline: His things are falling apart around him in rapid succession; he dramatically quotes Caesar at a pencil ('Et tu, pencil?') before sighing 'When it rains, it pours'
jokes.explanation: 'Et tu, pencil?' is a small gem — the Shakespearean betrayal register applied to a dropped pencil is perfectly absurd, and the deadpan 'When it rains, it pours' as a philosophical capper seals it. Garrett's existential suffering is played pitch-perfectly here.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: We face challenges every day. Financial struggles, academic pressures, questions about our futures...

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: We wonder if we're making the right choices.

dialogue.speaker: Troy Barnes
dialogue.line: If we're becoming the people we want to be.

dialogue.speaker: Abed Nadir
dialogue.line: But there's one threat that supersedes all of these concerns.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The Ass Crack Bandit.

jokes.text: Ass Crack Bandit! [crowd panics]
jokes.setup: Garrett's folders, pencils, and general misfortune have been cascading — then a coin drops down his butt crack
jokes.punchline: His anguished 'Ass Crack Bandit!' cry kicks off the entire episode's premise — his day going from bad to worse in the most absurd way possible
jokes.explanation: The cold open's entire comedic architecture — Garrett's escalating misery — is perfectly paid off by this single screamed phrase. The name itself ('Ass Crack Bandit') is an absurd maximalist crime-thriller label for the most trivially embarrassing crime imaginable. The structural economy is exceptional: three beats of mundane suffering culminating in this. It earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We need to address the gluteal cleavage situation immediately.

jokes.text: Raul Lopez, Las Noticias Hispanicas de Greendale. Will this affect soccer?
jokes.setup: Journalists are asking increasingly pointed questions about the Ass Crack Bandit
jokes.punchline: A reporter from a Spanish-language paper asks if the coin-dropping crime will affect soccer — a completely non-sequitur concern delivered with total journalistic seriousness
jokes.explanation: Five words do enormous work. The joke lives entirely in the gap between the question asked (will a coin-in-butt crime affect soccer?) and any rational connection. The addition of 'Las Noticias Hispanicas de Greendale' — a hyper-specific, bilingual community newspaper — makes it funnier by grounding the absurdity in Greendale's wonderfully ridiculous ecosystem.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Wait, we have more than one newspaper?

dialogue.speaker: Student Reporter 1
dialogue.line: The Greendale Gazette, sir.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Right, right.

dialogue.speaker: Student Reporter 2
dialogue.line: And The Community College Times.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh my god, how long has this been happening?

jokes.text: And how many photographs do you people need? / When did we split The Gazette from The Mirror?
jokes.setup: The dean is being swarmed by student journalists from multiple campus publications
jokes.punchline: He's bewildered that Greendale somehow has two separate student newspapers; his exasperation at the bureaucratic absurdity of his own school is relatable and funny
jokes.explanation: A quick background joke that works on the level of institutional absurdity — the dean doesn't even know his own school's newspaper situation. Functional but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: What's your stance on the new soccer field proposal?

dialogue.speaker: Raul Lopez
dialogue.line: I... we're in the middle of a campus security briefing.

jokes.text: Hanes His Ways.
jokes.setup: The dean reveals the Bandit's letter contained details about Garrett's underwear brand not known to the public
jokes.punchline: Garrett blurts out 'Hanes His Ways' — helpfully confirming it, apparently forgetting this is information he wasn't supposed to volunteer
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word joke. The setup is the dean saying the underwear brand is a secret detail; the punchline is Garrett immediately announcing it anyway, which is both a character joke (Garrett's haplessness) and an absurdist detail ('Hanes His Ways' — a real but hilariously specific product name). Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The bandit's letter says he robs banks to buy Hanes underwear.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Hence his ways.

jokes.text: The Bandit's letter: 'Humans make better banks than piggies. Whenever I get more change at the store, I can't wait to drop it down your butts. I think I will go to the bank and get so much change and make all my dollars into change and drop it all down there.'
jokes.setup: An ominous villain letter is being read aloud, crime-thriller style
jokes.punchline: The letter reads like a child wrote it — run-on sentences, childlike logic about banks, using 'butts' casually — subverting every serial-killer-letter genre expectation
jokes.explanation: The genre parody here is sharp: serial-killer correspondence is a thriller staple, and Community weaponizes the form by making the content disarmingly stupid and childlike. 'Make all my dollars into change' as a villain's manifesto is inspired absurdism. The escalating mundanity of the plan ('I will go to the bank') is expertly constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: This is barely literate. The formatting is atrocious. And he uses 'your' instead of 'you're.' Twice.

jokes.text: He should be called 'The Run-on Sentence Bandit.'
jokes.setup: The letter has just been read aloud — it's notably poorly written
jokes.punchline: Jeff's dry critique is purely grammatical rather than addressing the actual crime, which is a perfect character beat — he's the guy who notices style over substance
jokes.explanation: Jeff's critique of the villain's grammar rather than the crime is quintessential Jeff Winger — effortlessly cool, disengaged from actual concern, puncturing genre seriousness with superficiality. The reframe of 'Run-on Sentence Bandit' is a perfect deadpan rename. Very economic.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I want to assure you that security at Greendale is my top priority. We have state-of-the-art protocols in place.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I have no idea what those protocols are. I just nod when the security guy talks to me.

jokes.text: From this moment, people, we are at DEFCON 4 — if that's the highest DEFCON, and if high DEFCONs are worse than low ones.
jokes.setup: The dean is trying to deliver a dramatic threat-level declaration
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts it with his uncertainty about how DEFCON actually works — the parenthetical reveals he used the term for gravitas without understanding it
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining qualifier is a beautiful piece of character writing — the dean wants to project authority but can't stop himself from hedging. The joke works on two levels: (1) his incompetence, and (2) the meta-awareness that most people use DEFCON incorrectly (DEFCON 1 is actually most severe). The qualifier is what elevates this from a basic Dean joke to a great one.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: My mother's been ill. I've been taking care of her.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: But I've done my duty. Whether she makes it or not, that's on her now.

jokes.text: Hey, where'd you go? / I was taking care of my sick mother. She's still alive, but I've put in my time.
jokes.setup: Dean introduces Professor Duncan after an absence; Duncan offers a sympathetic excuse (sick mother)
jokes.punchline: He immediately deflates any sympathy with 'She's still alive, but I've put in my time' — framing elder care as a chore he's already adequately completed
jokes.explanation: This is sharp, dark writing. 'She's still alive, but I've put in my time' has the rhythm and economy of a great stand-up line delivered in character. It's pure Duncan — selfish, British, deadpan, cutting. The 'but' is doing incredible work: it concedes the lack of tragedy while asserting personal sacrifice anyway. This is one of the episode's best lines and justifies an 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Duncan, what did you have done? You look amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I was caring for my mother.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you went to Switzerland!

jokes.text: Britta. Oh, Pierce, good for you. I always thought that hairpiece was a bit cowardly.
jokes.setup: Duncan misidentifies Britta as Pierce, apparently confusing them
jokes.punchline: He then 'corrects' himself by complimenting what he thinks is Pierce's decision to stop wearing a hairpiece — the double insult lands on both characters simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Economically brutal: Britta is mistaken for Pierce (an insult to her), and Pierce's toupee is called 'cowardly' (an insult to him). Duncan's oblivious delivery is key. Good character work establishing Duncan's charming awfulness on his reintroduction.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: We've had our share of PR crises at Greendale. Remember when I accidentally approved the budget to build a statue of myself made entirely of marzipan? In July? In Arizona? The statue lasted three hours before it became a puddle of Dean-flavored disappointment.

jokes.text: Double fruit bonus. / Crikey! Kiwi combo, mate. / You can't handle the fruit.
jokes.setup: During a serious investigation briefing, background characters are playing a fruit-themed mobile game
jokes.punchline: Their excited commentary ('Double fruit bonus,' 'Kiwi combo, mate,' 'You can't handle the fruit') is completely disconnected from the serious conversation happening in the foreground
jokes.explanation: Classic Community background-gag layering. The rewatch bonus is real — attentive first-time viewers will catch it but it rewards careful viewing. 'You can't handle the fruit' is a good A Few Good Men parody. The gag recurs across the scene, earning 'running_gag' status.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is serious. We need to investigate who ate the last bagel. I'm going to document everything.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm playing Fruit Ninja now. HYAH! SLICE! The watermelon is destroyed! Another combo! Oh no, the banana got away! This is the most intense moment of my life!

jokes.text: My quickest time was 20 minutes. The A.C.B. did it in 10. So he's got long legs. I think he has something I don't — a shortcut.
jokes.setup: Annie presents her detective work: she sprinted between crime scenes to calculate the Bandit's speed
jokes.punchline: Her conclusion — 'he's got long legs... I think he has something I don't, a shortcut' — is delivered with complete procedural seriousness, as if this is legitimate crime investigation
jokes.explanation: Annie's overdedication to amateur sleuthing is her core character trait, and this is a good deployment of it. The 'long legs' conclusion followed by walking it back to 'shortcut' is a nice mini-misdirect. Character-dependent humor that works.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: This game is racist! The fruit is clearly biased against me!

jokes.text: Hey, Abed. Lab ran late. What'd Annie get us for dinner? I hope it's not salad again.
jokes.setup: Troy leaves a voicemail for Abed, treating their domestic arrangement with Annie with complete casualness
jokes.punchline: The casualness of the message — lab ran late, hope it's not salad — combined with the next line, is a sweet character beat about their found-family dynamic
jokes.explanation: More of a character/world-building moment than a pure joke, but the offhand domesticity is charming and mildly funny. Troy's salad complaint is relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Hey, uh, I was thinking we could grab dinner tonight. Maybe hit up that new place downtown? Or we could go to the meat store if you're in the mood for, uh, steaks or whatever. The meat store. Yeah.

jokes.text: I'd rather just stop at the meat store.
jokes.setup: Troy is voicing his preference for dinner alternatives to salad
jokes.punchline: 'The meat store' — not a butcher, not a deli, but specifically 'the meat store' — is a wonderfully childlike and Troy-specific way to refer to any place that sells meat
jokes.explanation: 'The meat store' is perfect Troy vocabulary. It captures his joyful, childlike relationship with language and food. Character integration is very high — this is a Troy Briggs line through and through. The absence of any self-consciousness about the phrasing is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what? In every movie, when someone's sad, they just throw a blanket over them and suddenly everything's better. But here's the thing — I'm still sad. The blanket didn't work. I think movies have been lying to us this whole time.

jokes.text: It's how they comfort victims in movies. / Okay, I am hereby banning change from this campus.
jokes.setup: Someone is being wrapped in a blanket and given a cup after being victimized
jokes.punchline: Abed's explanation that this is movie-victim protocol is funny on its own; the dean's response — banning all change from campus — is an absurd policy non-solution delivered with bureaucratic authority
jokes.explanation: Two good jokes in rapid succession: Abed's meta-awareness of movie tropes, and the dean's kneejerk policy overreaction. Both are well-characterized. The dean banning all currency is delightfully stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Effective immediately, I am banning all change from Greendale Community College campus.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, that's insane. What about people who need to do laundry?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: That's their problem. I want to hear what people think, and if they want to give me their two cents, they're going to have to give me actual pennies and nickels.

jokes.text: Guess what, your two cents is change — and it's banned.
jokes.setup: Someone starts to push back on the dean's change ban
jokes.punchline: The dean cuts them off with 'your two cents is change — and it's banned,' weaponizing the idiom 'putting in your two cents' as a policy enforcement tool
jokes.explanation: This is clever wordplay with genuine structural elegance. The idiom 'your two cents' (your opinion) becomes literally 'change' under the dean's new law — so he shuts down dissent with his own ridiculous rule. The double meaning is tight and the character use is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Ass Crack Bandit
dialogue.line: I know what you're thinking. How can someone with such a narrow entrance get in and out so quickly? The answer is simple: practice, dedication, and a strictly regimented diet of fiber supplements and prune juice.

jokes.text: Second letter: 'I hope you enjoyed my work again. You can't stop me, because what are you gonna do, not have butts?'
jokes.setup: Another Bandit letter is read with serious procedural weight
jokes.punchline: 'What are you gonna do, not have butts?' is an airtight logical defense — the villain has identified an unassailable vulnerability and states it with casual brilliance
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'What are you gonna do, not have butts?' applies genuine, unanswerable logic to an absurd premise — and it's right. It has the rhythm of a great comedy line, it's completely quotable, and it escalates the Bandit's characterization (childlike but somehow philosophically sound). The economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Dean, I have evidence that proves—

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: I'm going to stop you right there. According to subsection 12, paragraph B of the imaginary bylaws I just made up, anything you say is stupid and also you're stupid.

jokes.text: I beg your what? / I have evidence that shows I'm not listening. Exhibit A, exhibit B. [blocks ears]
jokes.setup: Annie tells the dean she thinks it's a teacher; he doesn't want to hear it
jokes.punchline: 'I have evidence that shows I'm not listening. Exhibit A, exhibit B' — he frames his own willful ignorance in the same evidentiary language used in investigations, and presumably physically demonstrates it
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: the dean adopts the investigation's own language to shut down the investigation. 'Exhibit A, exhibit B' as evidence of not-listening is a great internal logic joke. 'I beg your what' is also a fine standalone before the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Just take it easy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why? A quarter of a buck is still a quarter!

jokes.text: Okay, you wanna make trouble? Go to Parker Brothers. You're out.
jokes.setup: Annie pushes back and says the investigation will never end if he chooses politics over justice
jokes.punchline: 'Go to Parker Brothers' — Parker Brothers makes board games, most famously Monopoly, which is associated with fake money and the phrase 'make trouble' — it's a nonsensical dismissal that somehow makes internal sense as an insult
jokes.explanation: Mildly cryptic but rewarding — Parker Brothers connection to Monopoly (fake money/change) gives it a thematic layer. Mostly works as an absurdist non-sequitur dismissal. Rewatch value as viewers decode the connection.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not a psychologist. The guy steals things and wears a mask. That's literally it. Stop trying to make it deep.

jokes.text: Taking it easy is how Troy ended up with a quarter of a buck in his crack.
jokes.setup: Jeff tells Annie to 'take it easy' about the investigation
jokes.punchline: Annie weaponizes the Troy victim story to rebut Jeff's complacency — 'a quarter of a buck' is a hilariously precise dollar-fraction way to say 25 cents
jokes.explanation: Annie's rhetorical deployment of the Troy incident is good character work. 'A quarter of a buck' is an oddly formal/precise way to say 25 cents that adds a slight absurdist flavor.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No squealing? But that's my favorite part!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: *squeals excitedly*

jokes.text: The men on our coins understood that. Maybe the Ass Crack Bandit's point is we're letting our values slide.
jokes.setup: Annie is making a passionate speech about justice and civic responsibility
jokes.punchline: She pivots to a genuinely absurd interpretation of the Bandit's crimes as social commentary — 'the men on our coins' as moral exemplars, and the coin-in-butt as a metaphor for sliding values — delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Annie's earnestness is her defining comedic trait, and this is a peak deployment of it. The logic is internally coherent but insane: coins → founding fathers → moral values → values 'sliding' (like coins into cracks). The wordplay on 'slide' (values sliding/coins sliding) is embedded without being announced. Very well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.line: Safety pants! Get your safety pants here! Protect yourself from bandits with our reinforced denim!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How much are those?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.line: Forty dollars a pair.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Forty dollars? For pants?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.line: Safety pants. They're different.

jokes.text: Or maybe he's a frat boy coming from the Laundromat.
jokes.setup: Annie has just delivered a stirring speech about civic values and the Bandit as social commentator
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate deflation — the simplest, most mundane explanation delivered flatly — is the perfect comedic counterweight to Annie's grandiosity
jokes.explanation: Jeff's reductive pragmatism perfectly counterbalances Annie's idealism — this is their dynamic in a single line. The specificity of 'coming from the Laundromat' (coins! quarters!) makes it smarter than it first appears. It also lands a small procedural joke: Laundromats are the most logical source of a large quarter supply. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Singer
dialogue.line: It's a quarter to ass.

jokes.text: The important question is 'who cares?'
jokes.setup: Following Annie's passionate civic speech
jokes.punchline: Jeff's nihilistic dismissal of the entire crisis as unimportant is perfectly in character and lands as a comedic beat after the earnest speech
jokes.explanation: It's functional Jeff nihilism — the character works, the line is a little slight on its own but earns its laugh from context and delivery. Not a standout joke but serves its structural purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Based on the evidence, the bandit is either male or female, likely between the ages of 5 and 85. They probably have a face. They may or may not be wearing clothes. The bandit could be anyone in this room... or no one. They might strike again... or they might not.

jokes.text: Let me know what you need from me. On the down low. Way down low. [pause] And no squealing.
jokes.setup: Jeff agrees to help Annie investigate but wants to do it secretly
jokes.punchline: The triple escalation of 'on the down low... way down low... and no squealing' is a comedic rhythm gag — each addition is sillier and more emphatic, the last one ('squealing') adding a mob-movie flavor
jokes.explanation: Good comic rhythm — the pause before 'And no squealing' is perfectly timed. The escalating silliness of Jeff's conditions (he's terrified of being seen helping with something earnest) is a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You want me to use my powers? Fine. Here's what's going to happen: I'll make a reference to a TV show, everyone will laugh because they got it, and we'll all feel smart. Then I'll point out that my character exists only to make references, which is itself a reference to postmodern television. Then someone will say 'that's so Abed,' and we'll have achieved meta-comedy inception. But here's the thing—by acknowledging the trope, I'm not transcending it. I'm just another character in a show about characters who are aware they're in a show. We're all just doing what the writers want us to do. Even this speech. Especially this speech.

jokes.text: Okay, squeal.
jokes.setup: Jeff has just told Annie 'no squealing' as a condition of his help
jokes.punchline: He immediately invites her to tell him everything — the ironic self-contradiction delivered as a prompt is a crisp comedic reversal
jokes.explanation: Two-word callback punchline. 'Okay, squeal.' is the entire joke — the immediate abandonment of his stated condition. The economy is essentially perfect, and it works as a micro-callback to the line literally seconds before. Classic sitcom reversal in its most compressed form.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The problem with bad TV writing is it's not just intellectually offensive, it's physically painful. Like, my brain is literally rejecting it. I can feel synapses misfiring. This is what it must be like to be allergic to incompetence.

jokes.text: Real Neil here, five days into the return of the Ass Crack Bandit... Safety pants, 100 bucks a pop. / All sandwiches, $5. Sorry, no change. Blame the Bandit.
jokes.setup: A montage of the campus adapting to the Bandit's return
jokes.punchline: The campus economy has been distorted: 'safety pants' are being sold (a new product category), and the sandwich stand refuses to give change, blaming the Bandit — the crime has created a micro-economy
jokes.explanation: The 'no change, blame the Bandit' joke is the standout — it's the logical ripple effect of the crime wave, used as a commercial excuse, which is very funny. The 'safety pants' category creation is also a good world-building gag.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: If the decoy butt was free, then everything Chang owns is stolen.

jokes.text: The nature of the Ass Crack Bandit's crimes would suggest that he's angry or just fell in love. / We know that he hates money or loves it, or doesn't care about money and hates butts or loves them.
jokes.setup: Duncan is introduced as a criminal profiler who will help solve the case
jokes.punchline: His psychological profile covers every possible emotional motive with no exclusion — hate/love, money/no money, butts/no butts — rendering it completely useless as analysis
jokes.explanation: Brilliant satirical destruction of criminal profiling as a practice. By listing every possible emotional state as equally plausible, Duncan demonstrates that profiling is often just confidently-stated tautology. The structure escalates beautifully: angry OR in love → hates money OR loves it → doesn't care about money AND hates butts OR loves them. Each branch adds to the uselessness. Very well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Dear Greendale, you've been a real thorn in my side, but also a refreshing breeze that's been breathing down my neck.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Mixed metaphor. A thorn and a breeze are two completely different things. You can't be both a thorn in someone's side AND a breeze breathing down their neck. It's grammatically inconsistent and logically incoherent.

jokes.text: Abed, you're special. Can't you just stand at the scene of the crime and see what happened?
jokes.setup: Jeff addresses Abed as if he has actual psychic/detective abilities from TV shows
jokes.punchline: The ask that Abed 'stand at the scene and see what happened' treats him as a literal fictional detective, which Abed then plays straight — breaking the fourth wall of the genre parody
jokes.explanation: Setup for Abed's meta-commentary bit. Good character work — Jeff genuinely believes Abed might be able to do TV-detective things, which reveals how the group has absorbed Abed's media-literacy into their worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Ants don't have butts.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Yes they do. They have an abdomen.

jokes.text: I see a man using a social disorder as a procedural device. Wait, wait, wait — I see another man. Mildly autistic super detectives everywhere. Basic cable, broadcast networks.
jokes.setup: Abed 'does his thing' at the crime scene, and the expectation is he'll produce a Sherlock-style deduction
jokes.punchline: Instead he produces a media criticism: he identifies the 'mildly autistic super detective' as a TV trope saturating both cable and broadcast, calling himself and the genre out simultaneously
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's crown jewels. Abed's meta-commentary functions on three simultaneous levels: (1) it's a spot-on critique of the 'neurodivergent savant detective' TV trope (Sherlock, Monk, The Bridge, etc.), (2) it's Abed commenting on his own role in the show, and (3) it's the show itself critiquing the genre it's currently parodying. 'Basic cable, broadcast networks' as a punchline is devastating in its casual exhaustion. This is exactly what Community does at its best — the meta-awareness IS the joke, not a wink to it. Earns its 8.8.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Hey, Dave Matthews is a musical genius! The man plays violin AND sings. Do you know how hard that is? He's like if Mozart and a really attractive guy had a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And 'Crash Into Me'? That's not just a song, that's a transcendent experience. It's what plays in God's car when he's driving to work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You people wouldn't know artistry if it serenaded you with a jam band and made you feel feelings you didn't know you could feel.

jokes.text: Pain. Painful writing. It hurts.
jokes.setup: Abed continues his 'reading the crime scene' as a TV critic reading the script
jokes.punchline: His verdict on the 'mildly autistic detective' TV trope is simply 'Pain. Painful writing. It hurts.' — a critic's pan delivered as psychic vision
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure — 'Pain. Painful writing. It hurts.' — with escalating simplicity is exquisite. It's a TV critic's takedown compressed to six words, delivered by a character using TV-detective psychic vision powers to critique the TV-detective genre. The escalation from 'Pain' to 'Painful writing' to 'It hurts' mirrors the structure of piling-on critical disdain. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, so who here is a Dave Matthews fan? Anyone? Anyone at all?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, I guess that's the list.

jokes.text: Heartburn. It doesn't help me catch criminals.
jokes.setup: Dean asks Hickey 'what have you got?' in the classic procedural straight-man request for a report
jokes.punchline: Hickey misreads (or deliberately deflects) the question to report a physical ailment — and then clarifies it's not investigatively useful
jokes.explanation: Hickey's deadpan is well-deployed. The addition of 'It doesn't help me catch criminals' as a clarifying statement is the key — he's not making an excuse, just being precise. Classic deadpan structure: overly literal response + unnecessary clarification.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not comfortable with cameras in the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But I'm also not comfortable with getting assaulted in the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So I guess it's a wash.

jokes.text: Chang in a fake giant butt costume, saying 'You better put a quarter in that crack, Mr. Bandit.'
jokes.setup: The dean said he'd cook up a plan involving Chang; there's a dramatic build
jokes.punchline: Chang is deployed as a large fake butt as bait — the reveal of the costume is the visual punchline, and his line is a threat delivered while dressed as a butt
jokes.explanation: Visual comedy that lands primarily on the image — Chang in a giant butt suit is inherently funny. His threatening line ('You better put a quarter in that crack, Mr. Bandit') is funny because it invites the crime rather than deterring it. The rewatch bonus is the costume design.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Safety in numbers, people. That's why I always travel in groups of at least three.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: One to keep watch, one to keep... a... notch, and one to... spots... the... crotch!

jokes.text: I think it's spending too much money on a crime that nets you 25 cents a pop. / No, no. This was free. / Then I think you just admitted you already owned a fake butt.
jokes.setup: Jeff critiques the financial logic of the sting operation
jokes.punchline: The dean reveals the butt was free — implying he already owned one — and Jeff's immediate reframe ('you just admitted you already owned a fake butt') lands the actual punchline
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure with a perfect pivot. The first beat sets up a sensible financial critique. The second beat (free) seems to resolve it in the dean's favor. The third beat reframes the 'free' as evidence of a much more damning fact: the dean had a fake butt already. The audience has to do a beat of logic to fully land on the horror of the implication, which makes it even funnier. This is excellent comedic construction.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The teacher said he was at the science dance all night.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, if he was at the science dance all night, how come only one student showed up?

jokes.text: Third letter: 'I am the mad hatter, if hats were butts. I am neither left nor right. I am the space between. To me, you're all like ants marching to class, freaks on parade.'
jokes.setup: Another Bandit letter is read with crime-thriller gravitas
jokes.punchline: The letter now has literary pretensions — the 'mad hatter if hats were butts' metaphor, the pseudo-philosophical 'space between,' quoting what sounds like Dave Matthews lyrics
jokes.explanation: 'The mad hatter, if hats were butts' is a great line — a genuine attempt at metaphor that substitutes 'butts' for 'hats' with earnest pretension. The Dave Matthews connection becomes a clue. Rewatch bonus because the letter is a plot seed.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What? I'm eating with my real mouth.

jokes.text: I mean, why mix metaphors? Ants don't have butts. / Wait a minute. / Ants do have butts.
jokes.setup: Jeff critiques the Bandit's mixed metaphors in the letter
jokes.punchline: His critique ('ants don't have butts') is immediately corrected by Annie ('ants do have butts') — Jeff's confident wrong biology is funnier than if he'd been right
jokes.explanation: The setup baits the audience to agree with Jeff (he seems right), then Annie's factual correction flips it. Jeff's confident wrongness is more character-revealing than if he'd been right. The rhythm is tight. 'Wait a minute' selling that she's genuinely figured something out before landing the entomology fact is a lovely fake-out.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Bublitz
dialogue.line: This stuff is incredible. I mean, the flavor profile is complex — you're getting notes of citrus, maybe some pine. The high is very cerebral, very clean. No paranoia, no couch lock. And the ash? Silver. Silver ash, man.

jokes.text: Dave Matthews. Hard-core fans call him Dave.
jokes.setup: Someone identifies Dave as the artist — but just says 'Dave'
jokes.punchline: Shirley's clarification that hard-core Dave Matthews fans call him just 'Dave' is simultaneously an earnest fan-culture note and inherently funny because it's such a mundane familiarity — 'Dave' is the most common name
jokes.explanation: Functional gag that becomes important later (when it's used to identify Duncan). The humor is mild — the idea that calling a famous musician by his first name constitutes super-fan status is gently absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You can't suspend me.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Oh, I can't? Watch me. It's like those magazines quizzes: 'Which Douchebag Are You?' I'm all of them.

jokes.text: Oh, excuse me for being alive in the '90s and having two ears connected to a heart.
jokes.setup: Someone implies Shirley's Dave Matthews fandom is lame or dated
jokes.punchline: Shirley's defensive non-sequitur — 'two ears connected to a heart' — is a beautiful piece of earnest fan-speak that accidentaly reveals more than it defends
jokes.explanation: 'Having two ears connected to a heart' as a defense of one's taste is inspired. It's simultaneously meaningless and deeply felt — the anatomical precision ('two ears') combined with the emotional organ ('a heart') is absurd body-based sincerity. This is exactly the kind of line that gets quoted for years. Very Shirley and very quotable. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I've been observing you two, and what I'm seeing is a classic case of intellectual codependency masked as academic collaboration. Jeff, you're projecting your father issues onto Annie's need for validation, while Annie, you're unconsciously seeking a father figure through Jeff's superficial charm and emotional unavailability.

jokes.text: ['Done.'] — Thought that would take longer.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie need to assemble a list of Dave Matthews fans on the faculty — implying this will take time
jokes.punchline: One of them immediately says 'Done.' — the list was apparently trivially short or trivially easy, suggesting Greendale faculty's demographic is hilariously narrow
jokes.explanation: Classic 'expectation reset' joke — the audience assumes a research montage, the show skips it entirely with a single 'Done.' The two-word exchange is maximally efficient. The beat works by subverting the procedural genre convention of investigative labor.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Jeff, you're going to coach our water polo team as punishment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Water polo? Dean, I don't know anything about water polo.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, you're going to learn. And you're going to look *very* good in those tight coaching shorts.

jokes.text: Troy's Law: a camera in the bathroom is better than a quarter in your butt.
jokes.setup: The dean is presenting a new security measure to the school board
jokes.punchline: The 'law' named after Troy proposes bathroom surveillance as the solution — a horrifying privacy overreach justified by comparison to a relatively minor embarrassment
jokes.explanation: The slogan 'a camera in the bathroom is better than a quarter in your butt' is a solid absurdist policy joke. The implied harm equation (surveillance vs. minor embarrassment) is funny precisely because bathroom cameras are arguably worse. The naming of a civil-liberties-eroding law after a victim has political satire undertones.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We don't have romantic tension.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yeah, there's nothing there.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Absolutely nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Zero tension.

jokes.text: So please approve the dean's new security measure called Troy's Law...because a camera in the bathroom is better than a quarter in your butt.
jokes.setup: The dean is proposing a new security measure named after the original victim.
jokes.punchline: The measure is bathroom surveillance cameras, and his justification — 'a camera in the bathroom is better than a quarter in your butt' — presents privacy invasion as the preferable option.
jokes.explanation: Smart in its dark logic — the dean is proposing civil liberties violations as a lesser evil. The compare-and-contrast framing is clean and the specificity of both options makes it land. Also a subtle comment on post-9/11 security overreach applied to the most trivial possible 'threat.'

dialogue.speaker: Bandit
dialogue.line: You better watch your back, Dean. I know where you live.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Well, I appreciate the concern, but actually I've been meaning to tell someone—I've been going to a yoga class on Tuesday nights, and I think it's really changing my core strength. The instructor says I have natural flexibility for someone my age.

jokes.text: Bend over with friends over. There's safety in numbers.
jokes.setup: The dean is presenting the 'three B's' safety campaign: Belts, Briefs, and Buddies
jokes.punchline: 'Bend over with friends over' — a riff on 'come over with friends over' — the safety advice to never expose your crack while alone is delivered as a wholesome community slogan
jokes.explanation: 'Bend over with friends over' is a genuinely good slogan-joke — it has the rhythm of an anti-drug PSA slogan repurposed for butt-crack safety. The wordplay is clean and the community-safety register is well-sustained.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Greendale has stables?

jokes.text: [Community member gets cracked during the safety presentation] / He's under the bleachers! / Everyone remain calm, please! All right, free-for-all!
jokes.setup: The dean is literally mid-speech about Bandit safety
jokes.punchline: Someone gets cracked during the safety speech itself — the Bandit strikes at maximum irony — and the dean's 'Everyone remain calm... All right, free-for-all!' is an immediate, complete abandonment of composure
jokes.explanation: The structural irony of being victimized during a safety presentation is well-executed. The dean's instant pivot from 'remain calm' to 'free-for-all!' (a beat or two apart) is perfectly timed character collapse. His authoritarianism crumbles instantly under pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This place has the exact same creepy stable environment as my mother's house. Same lighting, same furniture, same smell of regret and horse feed.

jokes.text: I checked out Mrs. Plimpton. Airtight alibi. She's dead.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are comparing notes, crossing faculty suspects off their list
jokes.punchline: Jeff reports Mrs. Plimpton has an 'airtight alibi' — the reveal that the alibi is death is delivered with zero tonal shift, as if death is the most logistically convenient excuse
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark deadpan construction. 'Airtight alibi. She's dead.' — the buildup of 'airtight' followed by the most absolute possible alibi is a great two-beat. The absence of any reaction to this revelation (from Jeff or the narrative) makes it funnier. Death as procedural alibi is a great dark-comedy frame. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What are you doing out here?

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: I'm training horses to do my taxes.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: And teaching them to speak French. Also, I'm building a spaceship out of hay.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Starburns, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: Wait until you hear about my plans to marry the head horse and open a nightclub.

jokes.text: This extra long churro tastes good in my real mouth.
jokes.setup: Chang is wandering around the investigation in his butt costume
jokes.punchline: His unprompted clarification that he is eating a churro 'in my real mouth' (as opposed to, presumably, the fake butt-mouth of his costume) is a surreal specificity that raises more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: The key word is 'real' — the clarification implies there's a fake mouth in play (the costume butt), and that Chang felt the need to specify suggests he may have already eaten from the wrong one. It's a pure non-sequitur character beat that rewards contemplation. Chang's oblivious weirdness is perfectly deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: In Taiwan, we do it like this. Different countries, different high fives.

jokes.text: It's a mild, kind sativa, perfect for playing guitar.
jokes.setup: Bublitz has been caught after bolting; he's apparently holding marijuana
jokes.punchline: His unprompted product description of his weed — 'mild, kind sativa, perfect for playing guitar' — treats the substance as a legitimate consumer item with ideal use-cases rather than evidence of anything problematic
jokes.explanation: The connoisseur register — 'mild, kind sativa' — is funny because it's evaluative rather than defensive. 'Perfect for playing guitar' is a specific use-case recommendation that implies Bublitz has field-tested this across many musical instruments. Great character sketch in one line.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The evidence doesn't match up. The timeline is inconsistent, and the witness statements contradict each other.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I think what's really going on here is that you care about me. A lot.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? Jeff, focus—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, it's okay. I see it. And honestly, I'm flattered.

jokes.text: Annie, you're suspended. / Don't tell me what I can't do. / What do you think you are, Cosmo's July quiz?
jokes.setup: Jeff tells the dean he 'can't' suspend Annie
jokes.punchline: The dean retorts 'What do you think you are, Cosmo's July quiz?' — an utterly left-field reference implying Jeff's ability to tell someone what they can/can't do is as limited as a Cosmopolitan magazine personality quiz
jokes.explanation: 'Cosmo's July quiz' is a spectacularly specific and unexpected comeback. It works because the magazine quiz is famous for telling people what they 'are' (what type of person, lover, friend) — so the dean is saying Jeff has no more authority over reality than a magazine quiz does. The specificity of 'July' (not just any quiz — the July one) is a brilliant absurdist detail that makes it funnier without explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff, why did you touch my shoulder like that?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It was a supportive touch. Platonic. Entirely non-romantic and completely appropriate for a study group member to give to another study group member in a moment of emotional vulnerability.

jokes.text: I think you two like to partner up on cutesy capers so you can hold hands in the dark and address your urges in semi-acceptable scenarios.
jokes.setup: Dean observes Jeff and Annie's investigative partnership with suspicion
jokes.punchline: His analysis — 'hold hands in the dark and address your urges in semi-acceptable scenarios' — is both accurate (the Jeff/Annie dynamic is well-established) and brutally stated in bureaucratic register
jokes.explanation: 'Semi-acceptable scenarios' as a descriptor for their sleuthing partnership is excellent — it acknowledges the barely-sublimated tension while making the whole enterprise sound vaguely pathetic. The dean here is both accurate and unfair, which is funnier than being simply right.

dialogue.speaker: Student vendor
dialogue.line: Do you have any idea how much money you're throwing around like it's nothing?

dialogue.speaker: Student vendor
dialogue.line: This is actual currency! People work for this!

jokes.text: I'm punishing you, Jeffrey. Starting next week, you are the new coach of the water polo team. / Craig Pelton, dean and assistant water polo coach.
jokes.setup: The dean threatens Jeff with a 'punishment'
jokes.punchline: The punishment is becoming the water polo coach — which means Jeff has to work alongside the dean, who is already the assistant coach. The 'punishment' benefits the dean by giving him Jeff's company in a sport context
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the punishment is designed to put Jeff in the dean's orbit is classic Dean Pelton — his obsession with Jeff manifests even in disciplinary action. 'Craig Pelton, dean and assistant water polo coach' as a formal title announcement is a great comedic button.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I'm a huge Dave Matthews fan.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's streets ahead.

jokes.text: The Bandit calls the dean's office and says: 'I find it funny you ever thought you could catch me.'
jokes.setup: In full crime-thriller parody mode, the villain calls the investigation team
jokes.punchline: The Bandit's 'villain monologue' mimics every serial-killer movie call — but his taunts are fundamentally about a minor embarrassment crime rather than murders
jokes.explanation: The genre parody is sustained here — villain calling the cop is a thriller staple. The comedy derives from the disproportion between the villain's confidence and the crime. Rewatch value because the voice acting choice becomes a clue.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: David Lee Roth? Now that's a man who knew how to live. The guy had it all - the bandana, the splits, the screaming fans.

jokes.text: The Bandit asks if Jeff and Annie are chasing him as an excuse to get near each other. 'I mean, get a room already.' / We're friends!
jokes.setup: The Bandit monologues about observing Jeff and Annie's partnership
jokes.punchline: The Bandit voices the observation the dean just made — and the audience has long suspected — turning the villain into a Jeff/Annie shipper; the response 'We're friends!' is a protest too emphatic to be convincing
jokes.explanation: The Bandit as Jeff/Annie relationship commentator is a good meta move — the villain's observations echo the audience's and the dean's, making the unresolved tension the episode's real crime. 'We're friends!' as an unconvincing denial is classic.

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: I didn't not make that phone call.

jokes.text: I am the bringer of change. I am the filler of cracks. / Oh, that's very interesting. I myself was in 4H.
jokes.setup: The Bandit delivers a self-aggrandizing villain manifesto
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds to 'I am the bringer of change, I am the filler of cracks' with the completely non-sequitur 'I myself was in 4H' — as if sharing a biographical tidbit in response to a villain speech
jokes.explanation: 'I myself was in 4H' is a genuinely great line. It's Jeff continuing his stalling tactic by volunteering irrelevant personal information — keeping the Bandit on the line by turning the conversation into small talk. The specificity of '4H' (a rural agricultural youth club — very not-Jeff) makes it funnier and raises unanswerable questions about Jeff's childhood. This earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I saw some photos of you online.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: On FaceBrit.

jokes.text: Trace the call, Rhonda! This means trace the call!
jokes.setup: The dean needs Rhonda to trace the call; it should be obvious from context
jokes.punchline: 'This means trace the call' — the dean clarifies his instruction by literally stating what 'trace the call' means in the context of tracing a call, which is redundant and panicked
jokes.explanation: Good Dean Pelton bureaucratic panic. The clarification ('this means trace the call') is redundant by definition, suggesting either the dean doubts Rhonda or is simply catastrophizing. His inability to give a clean order under pressure is well-characterized.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I say, these laces require a minimum of seven-and-three-quarter inches of structural integrity to maintain proper pedestrian safety standards, as per the Royal Academy of Footwear Sciences.

jokes.text: Got it, the stables! We have stables?
jokes.setup: The trace returns a location: the stables
jokes.punchline: The dean's immediate incredulous 'We have stables?' is the comedic beat — he's discovering a feature of his own school during a criminal investigation
jokes.explanation: One of the best running jokes of Community — Greendale is so bizarre and poorly-managed that its own dean doesn't know its facilities. 'We have stables?' is a great character beat in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I'm bending down to tie my shoe in a way that respects the indigenous footwear traditions of the Pacific Northwest.

jokes.text: Add some doilies and a foot bath and this is my mom's house.
jokes.setup: The group arrives at the creepy stables hideout
jokes.punchline: Shirley's domestic interpretation of a crime scene hideout — identifying it as similar to her mother's home — reframes 'creepy' as 'cozy Southern grandmother'
jokes.explanation: Very Shirley — her domestic-homemaker perspective is her defining lens. The specific items ('doilies and a foot bath') are good character-specific details. The juxtaposition of crime den and grandmother's living room is effective.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: We need to find him before he gets away!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm on it! Which way did he go?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: According to my calculations, he's heading toward the library.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Then that's where we're going!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Excuse me, students. I have some terrible news.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What is it, Dean?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We just received word that Professor Professorson has passed away.

jokes.text: Mush! Mush! / No, run. Mush! / Star-Burns?
jokes.setup: Someone is fleeing through the stables
jokes.punchline: Star-Burns is apparently commanding what appears to be a sled team (or cats), and there's a debate about whether the command is 'mush' (sled) or 'run' — capping with the reveal that it's Star-Burns, presumed dead
jokes.explanation: The 'Star-Burns' revelation is the punchline to an extended cold-case mystery (he faked his death in an earlier season). The 'Mush/No, run/Mush' debate mid-chase is a good physical comedy confusion beat.

dialogue.speaker: Real Neil
dialogue.line: This is Real Neil from the radio, paying tribute to Pierce Hawthorne. He was like the dragon from our D&D campaign—old, powerful, and ultimately defeated by his own greed and lack of armor.

jokes.text: Since faking his death to escape meth charges, Alex 'Star-Burns' Osbourne has been living in the stables, eating garbage, and trying to build a cat car.
jokes.setup: Star-Burns is revealed as the stables inhabitant
jokes.punchline: The documentary-style title card narration recaps his circumstances with neutral journalistic detachment — 'eating garbage and trying to build a cat car' treated as equivalent life facts to escaping drug charges
jokes.explanation: The title-card format applied to Star-Burns's degraded circumstances is a great structural joke. 'Eating garbage' and 'trying to build a cat car' are presented with equal weight to the meth charges, suggesting the cat car is both aspirational and deeply concerning. The narration style itself is comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce may be gone, but he's still here in all of us. In our hearts, in our memories, in the way he taught us to live life to the fullest. And in his outstanding collection of racist memorabilia. Psssshhhhh!

jokes.text: High five? / Sure. / No. / Oh, American high five. Sorry.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie have apparently solved the case and go to high-five
jokes.punchline: The high five is aborted — they can't complete the gesture without it becoming 'hand-holding' (the dean's accusation), so they fumble; 'Oh, American high five. Sorry.' suggests they attempted a different cultural variant first
jokes.explanation: A clever callback to the dean's hand-holding accusation — now even a celebratory high-five is charged with the dean's framing. 'Oh, American high five. Sorry.' suggests they attempted a different version first (a hug? A European double-kiss?) — the specific apology implies a physical fumble we're meant to infer.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff, I'm worried this case is going cold.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Don't worry. I've got the killer instinct of a man on a mission.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Woman.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: A woman on a mission.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. [reaction beat to seeing Star-Burns revealed as the 'bandit']
jokes.setup: The case has been 'closed' — Star-Burns confessed
jokes.punchline: Someone's horrified reaction suggests the resolution is both anticlimactic and disturbing — they apparently expected something grander
jokes.explanation: Generic reaction beat. Without visual context it's hard to score highly — the comedy is in whatever they're seeing, not the exclamation itself.

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: So you give me money, and in return... you get absolutely nothing. No equity, no updates, no cat car rides. Just the knowledge that you helped make a dream real.

dialogue.speaker: Investor
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how crowdfunding works.

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: Isn't it though?

jokes.text: So much pain. But now it's time to heal! You're all invited to the official 'We Caught the Ass Crack Bandit' Dance tonight in the cafeteria!
jokes.setup: The dean has just acknowledged the community's suffering
jokes.punchline: His pivot from 'so much pain' to 'time to heal!' to hosting a celebratory dance named literally 'We Caught the Ass Crack Bandit Dance' is instant, undignified, and completely in character
jokes.explanation: The literal name of the dance ('We Caught the Ass Crack Bandit Dance') is the joke — it's the least elegant event name possible, delivered with the dean's characteristic over-enthusiasm. His emotional whiplash from grief to celebration is very Dean.

jokes.text: There's no way Star-Burns did it. Innocent people don't confess. / Are you kidding me? You knew it was a teacher. It doesn't add up.
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to close the case; Annie pushes back
jokes.punchline: 'Innocent people don't confess' — delivered by Jeff as a straight dismissal — is objectively wrong (innocent people confess all the time under pressure, as any criminal justice study shows), and Annie's immediate rebuttal implies she knows this too
jokes.explanation: Jeff's confident wrongness is a character staple — here his legal logic is hilariously backwards. It's also a mild procedural genre joke (the trope that confessions close cases, used in countless crime shows). Character-dependent.

jokes.text: Or maybe the dean was right about us. / What? No. Annie... I took this case because I wanted to help you. / Then what is this? / It's platonic shoulder holding.
jokes.setup: Annie raises the dean's accusation about their partnership being romantic cover
jokes.punchline: Jeff insists he helped because he cared about Annie — then when Annie gestures to whatever physical contact is occurring, he calls it 'platonic shoulder holding' — the most defensive possible descriptor for what is clearly not entirely platonic
jokes.explanation: 'Platonic shoulder holding' is a great phrase — the word 'platonic' is doing desperate work to neutralize an action that wouldn't need neutralizing if it truly were platonic. It's both funny and a genuine character beat in their ongoing dynamic.

jokes.text: It's a guy who puts quarters down butt cracks, Jeff. Let's just let it go.
jokes.setup: The case has stalled and Annie is exhausted; Jeff wants to pursue
jokes.punchline: Annie's pragmatic deflation of the entire investigation — 'it's a guy who puts quarters down butt cracks' — echoes Jeff's earlier dismissive tone, completing a character arc within the episode; she's become the pragmatist
jokes.explanation: This is a lovely structural callback — Annie's passionate believer becomes the deflater while Jeff becomes the pursuer. 'It's a guy who puts quarters down butt cracks' has the rhythm of Jeff's earlier dismissals but coming from Annie, it's both funny and character-revealing. The role reversal is the craft here, earning the 8.

jokes.text: Actually, would you mind coming to get me when Britta's drunk? / Yes! That is my jam right there.
jokes.setup: Duncan says he'll 'go to the dance later' — Jeff is about to deliver a flyer
jokes.punchline: He asks Jeff to alert him when Britta is drunk — confirming his interest in Britta is wholly opportunistic — and his exuberance at the music playing is a character beat that becomes a clue
jokes.explanation: Duncan's casual 'come get me when Britta's drunk' is both funny and characterologically precise — he wants Britta but only on favorable terms. The rewatch value is high because his music enthusiasm here is a clue to his identity as the Bandit.

jokes.text: Dave Matthews fan? / Obviously you're not. Real fans call him Dave.
jokes.setup: Jeff tests Duncan with the Dave Matthews clue from the Bandit's letter
jokes.punchline: Duncan's haughty correction — 'obviously you're not, real fans call him Dave' — mirrors Shirley's earlier fan-speak exactly, confirming Duncan as a Dave fan (and therefore a suspect)
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural callback — Shirley established the 'real fans call him Dave' rule and now it's the tool that fingers Duncan. The joke works both as a detective beat and as a callback to the fan-culture gag. The rewatch bonus is very high as viewers re-evaluate Duncan's earlier enthusiasm.

jokes.text: I've heard this song before. Winger, who is this? / What are you talking about? Don't know? / I remember it from the '90s. / It's Dave. / Lee Roth?
jokes.setup: Dave Matthews music is playing; Duncan and Jeff have identified it; Leonard chimes in
jokes.punchline: Leonard says he remembers it from the '90s but thinks 'Dave' refers to 'Lee Roth' (David Lee Roth, Van Halen) — the generational mismatch and wrong-Dave substitution is funny
jokes.explanation: Leonard's 'Lee Roth?' is a perfect misdirect on the Dave callback chain — a third character volunteering a completely wrong Dave. His generational wrong-Dave is in-character and the joke pays off the running Dave gag with a final unexpected twist.

jokes.text: You're not the Ass Crack Bandit. / Keep it down, huh? I made a deal with the dean. Said as long as I confessed, he'd let me slide on the meth and buy a space heater for my stable.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts Star-Burns about his confession
jokes.punchline: Star-Burns confirms the frame-up and reveals the bargaining terms — the meth charges AND a space heater. The 'space heater for my stable' as a negotiated settlement for a false confession is absurdly low-stakes
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Star-Burns falsely confessed for a space heater is characterologically perfect — he's so marginalized that creature-comfort bribery works. The pairing of 'dropped meth charges AND a space heater' (escalating from legal relief to mundane comfort) is funny in its specificity.

jokes.text: I got to go backstage once and meet the whole band. Everyone except Dave. / There's a whole album of photos online if you go to... You actually wouldn't be able to access it. I use an older, British form of Facebook called Mug-scroll.
jokes.setup: Duncan brags about his Dave Matthews band connection
jokes.punchline: His near-brag is immediately undercut: 'everyone except Dave.' Then he tries to prove it with photos but retreats to 'you couldn't access it' — his evidence is on 'Mug-scroll,' a fictional 'British Facebook'
jokes.explanation: 'Mug-scroll' is an inspired invention — a fictional social network that explains why no one can verify Duncan's story, with 'British' as the magic word that makes it both plausible and absurd. 'An older, British form of Facebook' treats nationality as a sufficient explanation for an impossible technology. The deflation of 'everyone except Dave' is also a great setup. This is excellent comedic invention. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: No, stay. We're just getting to know each other. / I really shouldn't, I have a... / Aren't you going to pick those up? [coins spill] / Yes. / Just reach down with your hand and... / Bye.
jokes.setup: Jeff is stalling Duncan; coins spill; Duncan bends to pick them up
jokes.punchline: Jeff encourages Duncan to reach down — deliberately engineering the conditions for a butt-crack exposure as a trap — and Duncan realizes just in time, saying 'Bye' and leaving
jokes.explanation: Jeff turning the Bandit's own method against him (engineering coin-pickup exposure) is a great structural reversal. The slow-burn of the trap being laid — 'just reach down with your hand and...' — builds to Duncan's abrupt 'Bye' as his self-preservation instinct kicks in. The suspense/comedy blend is well-executed.

jokes.text: This is the Ass Crack Bandit. I find it funny you ever thought you could catch me. / Jeff. / It's Duncan.
jokes.setup: The Bandit calls again with the same taunt
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Annie simultaneously recognize the voice is Duncan's — the reveal lands without fanfare, just two names
jokes.explanation: The reveal is elegant in its restraint — no dramatic music or monologue, just 'Jeff. It's Duncan.' The callback to the earlier identical phrase ('I find it funny...') creates the recognition moment. Economy is very high.

jokes.text: Annie? Jeff? Very nice. Oh, bloody hell, my shoe is untied — by British standards.
jokes.setup: Duncan has been caught at the scene; Jeff and Annie catch up to him
jokes.punchline: 'My shoe is untied — by British standards' — Duncan uses fake British-standards relativism to engineer a shoe-tying moment that exposes his crack for Annie to drop a coin in
jokes.explanation: 'By British standards' is a spectacular invention. It's Duncan using his nationality as a cover for the same coin-drop setup Jeff used against him — reversing the trap with a fake cultural excuse. The specificity ('by British standards' rather than just 'my shoe is untied') is what makes it brilliant. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, and structurally elegant as a reversal. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Shirley, what are you doing? / Looking for you. Did you see someone come this way? / Jeff, Annie, Pierce is dead.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are chasing Duncan through the dance
jokes.punchline: The chase is interrupted by Shirley delivering, mid-hunt, the news that Pierce has died — the tonal collision between butt-crack investigation and actual death is jarring and darkly funny in its timing
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most structurally interesting moments. The death of a major character (Chevy Chase's Pierce, an actual real-world exit from the show) is delivered as a tonal interruption of a slapstick chase. The writing doesn't milk it for drama or comedy — it just lands it, which is the right choice. Dark by restraint.

jokes.text: Pierce Hawthorne: 14-year Greendale student, entrepreneur, and expert heart attack faker — has passed away, for real this time.
jokes.setup: Announcement of Pierce's death
jokes.punchline: 'Expert heart attack faker — has passed away, for real this time' — the acknowledgment that Pierce had faked his death before is both a character-specific joke and a genuinely touching tragicomic note
jokes.explanation: 'For real this time' is a beautiful, painful, funny line. It acknowledges the fictional history of Pierce's fake death scares while confirming this one is genuine — without being sentimental or exploitative. The 'expert heart attack faker' as a formal credential on an obituary announcement is exactly the kind of Greendale joke that makes Community special. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: He's survived by many ex-wives and all of us here at Greendale that called him friend. If you're listening, Pierce — you were a hell of a D&D player. It's time to level up.
jokes.setup: Real Neil's on-air obituary for Pierce
jokes.punchline: 'It's time to level up' as a death sign-off is a D&D/gaming metaphor for dying that's both a nerd eulogy joke and a genuinely poignant send-off. 'Many ex-wives' is characterologically accurate and mildly funny.
jokes.explanation: 'Time to level up' is a perfect Community-brand sign-off for a character death — nerdy, game-reference-based, earned by the show's history. It's both a joke and a genuine goodbye. The 'many ex-wives' detail is Pierce in a nutshell.

jokes.text: Life is weird. It's a container for all this little stuff, and you get caught up in it. And then, the container just: [gesture]
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie process Pierce's death
jokes.punchline: Jeff's attempt at philosophical profundity trails off into a wordless gesture — his container metaphor collapses under its own weight, and he can't finish the thought
jokes.explanation: Jeff's gesture-punchline is a beautifully understated comedic moment. His attempt at wisdom is both sincere and funny — the unfinished container metaphor is exactly what someone would say while trying to seem profound. The gesture replaces the conclusion he doesn't have. Good character writing.

jokes.text: That hallway led to a dead end. We might've had him.
jokes.setup: In the wake of Pierce's death, Jeff talks about the investigation
jokes.punchline: Jeff returning to the Bandit investigation immediately after the emotional Pierce conversation is both funny and sad — his emotional processing includes redirecting to a minor crime
jokes.explanation: Jeff's immediate pivot back to the Bandit investigation after the Pierce moment is emotionally revealing in a comedic way — he can't sit with grief, so he redirects to an inconsequential mystery. It's a deft character beat.

jokes.text: The case goes cold again.
jokes.setup: The episode appears to be ending without resolution
jokes.punchline: The narrator/Abed's flat declaration — 'The case goes cold again' — treats the unresolved mystery as a genre expectation fulfilled. The Bandit is never caught, the ending is ambiguous, the procedural parody is completed.
jokes.explanation: Five words that complete the episode's genre parody architecture. 'The case goes cold again' has the resonance of a crime documentary's closing sentence — melancholy, resigned, final. It earns its structural placement as the narrative button. The word 'again' is crucial — it implies this has happened before and will happen again, which is both funny (the crime is so minor) and thematically resonant.

jokes.text: Don't worry. I got a feeling he'll be back. / Or her.
jokes.setup: Abed predicts the Bandit will return
jokes.punchline: Annie's 'or her' — an afterthought gender-correction that also reopens the mystery and subverts the assumed male-villain trope — is a small but effective beat
jokes.explanation: 'Or her.' — two syllables, delivered as an afterthought, that reopen the entire mystery. It reframes every previous 'he' in the investigation, invites rewatch, and subverts the serial-killer trope's gender assumption. Economically excellent.

jokes.text: Star-Burns's cat car Kickstarter video: 'You know, climate change is threatening our world, but there is a solution: the cat car. The world's first animal-powered vehicle. My original prototype was hunger-based. But sometimes, cats aren't hungry.'
jokes.setup: Post-credits tag: Star-Burns has made a crowdfunding video for his cat car
jokes.punchline: The 'hunger-based prototype' — a vehicle that moves when a cat chases food — is an engineering concept so fundamentally flawed that the inventor's calm acknowledgment of its failure ('but sometimes, cats aren't hungry') is perfect
jokes.explanation: 'But sometimes, cats aren't hungry' as an engineering problem statement is inspired. The calm acknowledgment that the entire first prototype failed on the most basic behavioral variable of cats is delivered with complete investor-pitch sincerity. The cat car premise is absurdist gold, and the execution here is excellent. 'Sometimes, cats aren't hungry' deserves to be quoted forever.

jokes.text: My new model will use a rear-fixed dog system. But dogs cost money, your money. By donating to this project, you'll be like an investor...except without taking all my profits.
jokes.setup: Star-Burns describes the improved cat car model that uses a 'rear-fixed dog system.'
jokes.punchline: 'You'll be like an investor, except without taking all my profits' — this is simultaneously a terrible deal for investors AND a confession that he has thought through the financial arrangements in his favor.
jokes.explanation: 'Like an investor, except without taking all my profits' is a gem. It describes a donation with a straight face, as if the lack of return makes it more appealing. The 'rear-fixed dog system' is also good engineering language applied to tying a dog to a cat car.

jokes.text: My new model will use a rear-fixed dog system. But dogs cost money, your money. By donating to this project, you'll be like an investor — except without taking all my profits.
jokes.setup: Star-Burns pivots from the failed cat prototype to the new dog system
jokes.punchline: 'You'll be like an investor — except without taking all my profits' — he correctly describes crowdfunding as investor-like but adds the crowdfunder's key advantage (no profit-share) with apparent pride, as if this is a generous offer to backers
jokes.explanation: 'You'll be like an investor, except without taking all my profits' is a perfectly constructed absurdist line. It accurately describes crowdfunding's value proposition from the fundraiser's perspective — framed as a benefit to donors — which is both a sharp satire of crowdfunding culture and a great character beat. The 'except' is doing all the work. Highly quotable. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Donate $5, get a thank-you e-mail. Fifty dollars gets you a T-shirt. One hundred gets you a T-shirt and a thank-you e-mail.
jokes.setup: Star-Burns lists the tier rewards for his crowdfunding campaign
jokes.punchline: The $100 tier rewards — 'a T-shirt AND a thank-you e-mail' — are simply the $5 and $50 rewards combined, with zero additional value. The escalation goes: email → shirt → email + shirt, as if 'email + shirt' justifies 20x the price
jokes.explanation: The crowdfunding tier structure joke is perfectly engineered. The $5 tier: email. The $50 tier: shirt. The $100 tier: shirt + email = exactly what you get for $55. The logic is airtight in its absurdity — he's just bundling the previous tiers and charging 20x more. The structure is 10/10 and the economy is near-perfect. This is one of the episode's funniest jokes and an excellent send-off for the tag.

jokes.text: Donate $5, and you get a thank-you e-mail. Fifty dollars gets you a T-shirt. One hundred gets you a T-shirt and a thank-you e-mail.
jokes.setup: Star-Burns lays out the Kickstarter reward tiers.
jokes.punchline: The $100 tier gives you exactly what the $5 and $50 tiers give separately — a T-shirt AND a thank-you email — making the top tier worth less per dollar than the lower tiers combined.
jokes.explanation: The structure is meticulous and perfect: $5 = email, $50 = T-shirt, $100 = T-shirt + email. The top tier is simply the combination of the two lower tiers with no escalating value. The joke works because (a) the internal logic is consistent — he's not random, he's genuinely thought this through badly, and (b) the escalation structure primes you to expect something better at $100. The reveal that $100 tier is just the previous two combined is a structural joke that requires careful construction. One of the episode's most technically accomplished comedy moments.

tmdb_overview: With the mysterious Ass Crack Bandit back at Greendale, Annie and Jeff are on the case. As clues and suspicions mount, Shirley delivers shocking news.
insight: Butt-coin heist episode mines 61 jokes in 45 minutes—absurdist comedy at peak density.
